prompt.context: Our client is a Real Estate Construction Services company with $6 billion in revenues. Its legal expenses are $30 million. In spite of these high legal expenses, a large percentage of judgments have NOT gone in its favor in the past two years. Our client would like us to diagnose and offer a solution to their problems.
prompt.question: How would you go about diagnosing the problems? What info do you need? How would you collect it? What are the problems? What recommendations do you have?

clarifying_info.q: How is the legal department structured?
clarifying_info.a: There are 25 lawyers in the company who work on 2 types of operations: Contract Review and Dispute Resolution.

clarifying_info.q: How is the $30 million in legal expenses broken down?
clarifying_info.a: $27 million is external legal counsel (300 legal suppliers) and $3 million is internal legal counsel.

clarifying_info.q: Has the nature of litigation changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: We have seen an increase in the number of fixed government contracts and consequently the litigations associated with such contracts.

clarifying_info.q: What portion of external spend is for litigation?
clarifying_info.a: 90% of external spend is for litigation and dispute resolution.

clarifying_info.q: How does our legal spend compare to industry benchmarks?
clarifying_info.a: Companies with similar revenue spend 0.1% of revenue on litigation. Construction companies spend 0.25% of revenue on litigation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the typical internal vs external spend ratio for top construction companies?
clarifying_info.a: Top 50% of construction companies have a mix of 6:1 External:Internal legal spending.

clarifying_info.q: How concentrated is our external supplier base?
clarifying_info.a: 80% of our external spending goes to 30 suppliers; for the rest of the industry the equivalent is 10 suppliers.

framework: Understand current legal spend structure: internal vs. external split, types of work (Contract Review vs. Dispute Resolution)
Benchmark against industry: compare spend as % of revenue and internal/external ratio to peers
Diagnose root cause of poor judgment outcomes: quality of external counsel, internal oversight, nature of cases (fixed government contracts)
Evaluate supplier base: 300 suppliers vs. ~10 for top industry peers suggests fragmentation and lack of preferred-provider relationships
Develop recommendations: consolidate supplier base, increase internal capacity or oversight, implement contract review process improvements

questions.prompt: How does the client's legal spend compare to industry benchmarks?
questions.guidance: Client spends $30M on legal. Revenue is $6B. Legal spend as % of revenue = 30/6000 = 0.5%. Industry average (similar revenue) is 0.1%; construction industry average is 0.25%. Client spends 2x the construction industry average and 5x the general industry average, indicating overspend.

steps: Client is spending $30M vs. $15M benchmark — 2x overspend vs. construction peers
math.answer: Client spends 0.5% of revenue on legal, vs. 0.25% for construction peers — approximately $15M in excess spend

questions.prompt: Is the internal vs. external legal spend ratio appropriate?
questions.guidance: Client ratio is $27M external : $3M internal = 9:1. Top 50% of construction companies maintain 6:1. Client's ratio is significantly higher, suggesting over-reliance on external counsel and under-investment in internal capability, which likely drives both higher cost and worse outcomes.

steps: Excess external spend implied: if client matched 6:1 ratio on same total, internal = ~$4.3M, external = ~$25.7M — directional, not definitive
math.answer: Client ratio is 9:1 vs. 6:1 benchmark, indicating over-reliance on external counsel

questions.prompt: Is the supplier base appropriately concentrated?
questions.guidance: Client uses 300 suppliers and 80% of spend goes to 30 suppliers. Industry uses ~10 suppliers for the equivalent concentration. The fragmented tail (270 smaller suppliers) adds complexity, reduces volume leverage, and likely dilutes quality oversight. Consolidating to a preferred provider panel of ~10 would mirror best practice.

steps: Remaining 20% = $5.4M spread across 270 suppliers = $20K average each
Fragmentation risk: no volume leverage on the tail
math.answer: Client uses 30 suppliers for core spend vs. ~10 for industry best practice — 3x more fragmented

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to reduce legal costs and improve judgment outcomes?

categories.name: Supplier consolidation
ideas: Reduce external panel from 300 to ~10-15 preferred providers
Negotiate volume-based rate agreements with panel firms
Implement performance tracking (win rates, cost per case) for external counsel

categories.name: Internal capability
ideas: Increase internal legal headcount to bring ratio closer to 6:1
Establish dedicated in-house specialists for fixed government contract litigation
Improve internal Contract Review process to catch issues before litigation

categories.name: Process improvement
ideas: Implement early dispute resolution / alternative dispute resolution (ADR) to reduce litigation
Create structured intake and triage process for legal matters
Track judgment outcomes by case type, supplier, and contract type to identify patterns

categories.name: Government contract management
ideas: Given increased government contracts, hire counsel with specific government contracting expertise
Build internal knowledge base for fixed-price government contract terms and risk clauses
Proactively review contract terms pre-execution to reduce downstream disputes

recommendation: Consolidate external counsel from 300 to ~10-15 preferred providers with performance-based agreements to improve quality and reduce cost
Increase internal legal capacity to move toward industry 6:1 external:internal ratio, particularly for government contract work
Implement structured contract review and early dispute resolution processes to reduce litigation volume
risks: Transition risk during supplier consolidation — active cases must be managed carefully during handoff
Internal hiring takes time; short-term cost savings may be offset by recruitment and onboarding costs
Government contract litigation may remain elevated regardless of internal improvements if contract terms themselves are unfavorable
next_steps: Conduct detailed spend analytics across all 300 suppliers to identify consolidation candidates
Benchmark win rates by external counsel firm to identify highest-performing partners
Map internal legal workflows to identify contract review gaps that are leading to disputes
